p9-1.a: Synchronously within the request, because files are capped at [5 MB, about 10,000 rows] and parsing is streamed, so validation finishes in [a few seconds] and users get the preview immediately. The I/O is fully async (async/await). For much larger files I would switch to a background job returning 202 and a job id.
p9-1.qa: Synchronously within the request, because files are capped at [5 MB, about 10,000 rows] and parsing is streamed, so validation finishes in [a few seconds] and users see the preview immediately. All I/O is async, so no threads are blocked; for much larger files I'd switch to a background job with 202 Accepted and a status endpoint.
i: Measured worst case at the size limit before choosing synchronous.
Request timeout and size limits protect the server.
Trade-off: simpler UX and code now vs scalability later.
f: What was the slowest part?
Duplicate checks against the database, solved by loading lookups once.
When would you go async?
When files grow beyond what fits comfortably within a request timeout.
wv: I choose the simplest design that meets measured needs.

p9-2.a: Authorised endpoint with role checks per study; size limit and .csv extension plus content check; files processed in memory or temp storage, never executed or served back; CSV-injection protection when exporting error reports; antivirus scanning per platform policy; every import audited with user and import id.
p9-2.qa: An authorised endpoint with role checks per study; a size limit and .csv extension plus content checks; files processed in memory or temp storage, never executed or served back; CSV-injection protection when exporting error reports; and an audit of who uploaded what.
i: CSV injection: prefix cells starting with =, +, -, @ (and tab/CR) with a quote when exporting.
Reject binary content by checking it parses as text CSV.
Antivirus scanning for stored uploads.
Uploads are capped at [5 MB] with request size limits configured on the endpoint.
f: What is CSV injection?
Spreadsheet formulas in cells that execute when opened in Excel.
Why not store uploads?
Less attack surface and less sensitive data at rest.

p9-3.a: Streamed parsing with CsvHelper instead of loading the file; validation in stages with early stop on header errors; database lookups (existing sites, countries, depots) loaded once into dictionaries instead of per row; batched inserts inside one transaction; AsNoTracking for reads.
p9-3.qa: Streamed parsing with CsvHelper instead of loading the whole file; validation in stages with an early stop on header errors; database lookups (existing sites, countries, depots) loaded once into dictionaries instead of per row; batched inserts inside one transaction; and AsNoTracking for reads.
i: HashSet for in-file duplicate detection: O(n).
Avoid per-row SaveChanges; one SaveChanges with batching.
Measured: [10,000 rows in a few seconds].
f: Why dictionaries?
O(1) lookups instead of a query per row (N+1).
Biggest win?
Removing per-row database lookups.

p9-4.a: Unit tests per validation rule (missing fields, bad types, duplicates in file and database, invalid country or depot); integration tests saving a file into a test database and checking rollback on failure; Playwright E2E tests for upload, preview and confirm; FV with large and broken files.
p9-4.qa: Unit tests per validation rule (missing fields, bad types, duplicates in file and database, invalid country or depot); integration tests saving a file into a test database and checking rollback on failure; Playwright end-to-end tests for upload, preview, error download and confirm; plus a test at the maximum file size.
i: Test data files checked into the repo for repeatability.
FV scripts reused the same scenarios.
Unit tests for the parser and each validation rule with good and bad rows; integration tests with real SQL Server for the transaction.
Edge cases: empty file, header only, [~10,000] rows, BOM, quoted commas, and duplicate site numbers.
f: How did you test rollback?
Inject a failure mid-save and assert no rows were written.
How did you test performance?
A generated 10,000-row file timed in integration tests.

p9-5.a: Only one import per study at a time, enforced with a lock row checked inside the transaction; a second user gets a clear 'import in progress' message; the file hash also blocks the same file being imported twice.
p9-5.qa: Only one import per study at a time, enforced with a lock row checked inside the transaction; a second user gets a clear "import in progress" message; the file hash blocks the same file being imported twice; and a [concurrency limit of 2 imports per user] protects the server.
i: sp_getapplock is an alternative for app-level locks in SQL Server.
Lock released in finally or by transaction end; stale locks expire.
Tested with two parallel imports for the same study: one succeeds, the other gets the friendly message.
The per-user limit returns 429 with a clear message.
f: Why per study?
Two imports into one study could conflict on duplicates and rules.
What if the server crashes holding the lock?
The lock is tied to the transaction or has an expiry, so it releases.

p9-6.a: Nothing is saved: all rows are written in one transaction, so any failure (database error, timeout) rolls everything back; the user sees an error and can retry; the audit log records the failed attempt.
p9-6.qa: Nothing is saved: all rows are written in one transaction, so any failure (database error, timeout) rolls everything back; the user sees an error and can retry; and the audit log records the failed attempt.
i: Execution strategy with retries wraps the whole transaction for transient errors.
Idempotent retry thanks to the file hash check after rollback.
Validation happens before the transaction, so most failures are caught with a full error report and nothing is written.
For millions of rows, a staging table with batch commits would replace the single transaction.
f: Is a long transaction a problem?
For 10,000 rows it's seconds; for millions, use staging tables.
What does the user see?
A clear message and the option to retry; no partial data.

p9-7.a: Upload directly to S3 with a presigned URL; a background worker (ECS or Lambda) streams and validates in chunks; stage rows in a staging table with SqlBulkCopy; validate set-based in SQL; then merge into live tables in controlled batches; progress via job status; errors written to a downloadable report.
p9-7.qa: Upload directly to S3 with a presigned URL; a background worker (ECS or Lambda) streams and validates in chunks; stage rows in a staging table with SqlBulkCopy; validate set-based in SQL; then merge into live tables in controlled batches, reporting progress and an error file, with idempotency by file hash and job id.
i: Step Functions or a job table to orchestrate stages.
Parallel chunk processing into staging.
Notify via email or SignalR when done.
Upload to S3, process asynchronously with SqlBulkCopy into a staging table, validate in set-based SQL, then merge in batches with progress reporting.
f: All-or-nothing at that scale?
Use staging so live data changes only after full validation, then a final merge.
Why SqlBulkCopy?
Orders of magnitude faster than row inserts.

p9-8.a: Unit tests for each of the five checks, pass and fail (live study with randomized subjects, version mismatch, wrong direction, transfer in progress, missing role or change request); integration tests for the transaction and lock with two concurrent transfers; FV scripts with evidence.
p9-8.qa: Unit tests for each of the five checks, pass and fail (live study with randomized subjects, version mismatch, wrong direction, transfer in progress, missing role or change request); integration tests for the transaction and lock; tests that every attempt is audited; and FV scripts covering each blocking scenario.
i: Concurrency test: two transfers at once, only one proceeds.
Fail-closed test: a check that throws blocks the transfer.
Tests ran in CI and as part of FV evidence for validation.
Regression tests added for every bug found in UAT.
f: Why test fail-closed?
An exception must never let an unsafe transfer through.
How did you get test data?
Seeded studies in each state in the test database.

p9-9.a: Every attempt, allowed or blocked, writes an audit record: user, source and target study and environment, change request reference, which check failed and why, timestamp. Validators and support can report on blocked attempts.
p9-9.qa: Every attempt, allowed or blocked, writes an audit record: user, source and target study and environment, change request reference, which check failed and why, and timestamp. Validators and support can report on blocked attempts, and repeated blocks trigger follow-up.
i: Audit written even when the transfer is blocked (separate from the transfer transaction).
Structured reasons enable reporting.
Audit records are append-only and can't be edited by application users.
Blocked attempts are reviewed in support reports.
f: Why audit allowed attempts too?
Full traceability of every transfer for inspections.
Who reviews blocked attempts?
Support and the study configuration team.

p9-10.a: Bringing together every team's changes for a release (application, APIs, database scripts, UI), merging them into the release branch, resolving conflicts, tagging one version and producing a consistent set of artifacts for validation.
p9-10.qa: Release integration brings together every team's changes for a release (application, APIs, database scripts, UI), merges them into the release branch, resolves conflicts, tags one version and produces a consistent set of artifacts for installation and validation.
i: Checklist per item: merged, tested, config changes, DB scripts, release notes.
Daily integration builds catch conflicts early.
Merging work from [5] teams into one release branch, building and installing it in test environments, and coordinating fixes before FV.
f: Biggest risk?
Late merges and environment configuration differences.
Tools used?
Azure DevOps branches, tags, pipelines and the MCP server.
wv: I bring structure to multi-team delivery.

p9-11.a: Validate: automated tests, smoke tests after install, version checks on every node, FV scripts with evidence, UAT sign-off.|Promote: the same tagged artifacts that passed UAT go to production under an approved change request, deployed by TechOps or the controlled pipeline in the agreed window, followed by verification.

steps.title: Tag + build
steps.detail: One version for app, API, DB, UI

p9-11.qa: Validation uses automated tests, smoke tests after install, version checks on every node, FV scripts with evidence and UAT sign-off. Promotion takes the same tagged artifacts that passed UAT to production under an approved change request, deployed by the controlled pipeline with verification afterwards.
i: No rebuilds between environments.
Evidence archived with the release record.

Release manager and QA per change control.

p9-12.a: One release version and checklist; order of deployment: backward-compatible database scripts first, then APIs, then application services, then UI; feature flags for incomplete work; a daily status check with each team before FV.
p9-12.qa: One release version and checklist; deployment order: backward-compatible database scripts first, then APIs, then application services, then UI; feature flags for incomplete work; and a daily status check with each team before the release.
i: Expand/contract DB changes keep old and new code working.
Contract tests between UI and APIs.
Order: database scripts first (backward-compatible), then APIs, then UI, with feature flags for incomplete features.
A release plan with owners and rollback steps per component.

New code may need new columns; old code tolerates them if additive.
How do you handle a late UI change?
Feature flag it off or move it to the next release.

p9-13.a: Our nodes run Linux-based install steps where Shell is natural; Python handles logic such as reading manifests, comparing versions and calling APIs; with Ansible they make installs repeatable and identical on every node, and the MCP tools call the same scripts.
p9-13.qa: Our nodes run Linux-based install steps where Shell is natural; Python handles logic such as reading manifests, comparing versions and calling APIs; with Ansible they make installs repeatable and identical on every node, removing manual steps.
i: Idempotent scripts; set -euo pipefail in Shell.
Python for anything beyond simple command sequences.
Ansible, Python and Shell were already used for installation on Linux nodes; scripts are easy to version and review.
Python for parsing and validation, Shell for system tasks.
f: Why not PowerShell?
The nodes are Linux; Shell and Python are native there.
How do you test scripts?
Run in a test environment and use shellcheck and pytest.

p9-14.a: Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell run the install steps across [4 to 6] nodes in order, stopping on failure.|Version consistency: every node reports its installed version (version file and health endpoint) and a check compares them with the release tag; any mismatch fails verification.
p9-14.qa: Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell run the install steps across [4 to 6] nodes in order, stopping on failure. Every node reports its installed version (version file and health endpoint), and a check compares them with the release tag; any mismatch fails verification.
i: serial: 1 for rolling installs; any_errors_fatal to stop.
The MCP version-check tool automates the comparison.
Release stages run install scripts on each node; a version-check tool compares versions across all nodes at the end.
A failed node can be retried alone after a fix.
f: What if one node fails?
Stop, fix, rerun that node (Part 3 Q27).
Why check versions explicitly?
A silently failed copy can leave a node on the old version.

p9-15.a: Version check on every node, health endpoints green, smoke tests of key flows (login, randomize in a test study, shipment list), logs and dashboards free of new errors, then sign-off in the release record.
p9-15.qa: Version check on every node, health endpoints green, smoke tests of key flows (login, randomize in a test study, shipment list), logs and dashboards free of new errors, then sign-off in the release record.
i: Compare error rates before and after.
Automated smoke tests where possible (Playwright).
Smoke tests, health endpoints, version checks across nodes, and log review for errors after deployment.
Grafana dashboards and CloudWatch Logs Insights for the first hours.
f: How long do you watch after release?
[An agreed window, e.g. the first hours of business use].

Failed smoke tests or error spikes linked to the release.

p9-16.a: Agile: deliver in small increments, get feedback often and adapt.|Scrum: fixed-length sprints with roles, planning, review and retrospective.|Kanban: continuous flow with work-in-progress limits and no sprints; good for support and operations work.
p9-16.qa: Agile means delivering in small increments, getting feedback often and adapting. Scrum uses fixed-length sprints with roles (product owner, scrum master, team), planning, review and retrospective; Kanban uses continuous flow with work-in-progress limits and no sprints, good for support and operations.
i: Scrumban mixes both.
Metrics: velocity (Scrum), cycle time and throughput (Kanban).
Scrum: fixed sprints, roles and ceremonies; Kanban: continuous flow with WIP limits.
Our team used Scrum with [two-week] sprints; release integration work fits Kanban.
f: When choose Kanban?
Unpredictable incoming work like support.
What is WIP limit for?
Reducing multitasking and exposing bottlenecks.

p9-17.a: Planning: the team picks prioritised, groomed stories that fit its capacity, agrees a sprint goal and breaks stories into tasks.|Retrospective: at the end of the sprint, the team discusses what went well, what did not and agrees one or two improvements to try.
p9-17.qa: In sprint planning the team picks prioritised, groomed stories that fit its capacity, agrees a sprint goal and breaks stories into tasks. A retrospective at the end of the sprint discusses what went well and what didn't, and agrees one or two improvements to try.
i: Capacity accounts for leave, support rotation and release work.
Retro formats: start/stop/continue, 4Ls.
Planning: commit to sprint goals and stories with estimates including validation effort.
Retrospective: what went well, what didn't, and one or two actions with owners.
f: What makes a good sprint goal?
A single outcome that gives the sprint focus.
How do you ensure retro actions happen?
Put them on the board with owners.

p9-18.a: Clarify the reason and impact with the product owner and BA, estimate the change, agree what moves out of the sprint, update acceptance criteria and traceability (important in GxP), and design code to be easy to change (clean boundaries, tests).
p9-18.qa: Clarify the reason and impact with the product owner and BA, estimate the change, agree what moves out of the sprint, update acceptance criteria and traceability (important in GxP), and design code to be easy to change (clean boundaries, tests).
i: Protect the sprint goal; renegotiate scope transparently.
Clarify the reason for the change and its priority with the product owner.
Assess impact on the sprint and GxP documentation, then agree what moves out.
Keep changes visible on the board so nobody is surprised.
f: What if it's urgent?
Swap equal-sized work out with the product owner's agreement.
GxP impact?
Requirements, tests and traceability must be updated together.

p9-19.a: Review for correctness, security, readability, tests and design, in small pull requests; comment on code not people, explain why, separate must-fix from suggestions.|Disagreement: discuss with data (benchmarks, docs, team standards), talk briefly in person if comments go back and forth, and involve the lead or agree a team rule if still stuck.
p9-19.qa: I review for correctness, security, readability, tests and design, in small pull requests; comment on code not people, explain why, and separate must-fix from suggestions. For disagreement I discuss with data (benchmarks, docs, team standards), talk briefly in person if comments go back and forth, and involve the lead or agree a team rule if still stuck.
i: Prefix comments: "nit:", "blocking:".
Automate style with analyzers so reviews focus on substance.
Disagreements: discuss the trade-off with data, prefer team standards, and escalate to a quick call rather than long comment threads.
f: How fast do you review?
[Usually the same day].
What do you look at first?
Tests and the riskiest changes.
wv: I keep reviews constructive and focused on quality.

p9-20.a: Situation: release deployments needed about 6 people and 6 hours.|Task: I proposed automating them through an MCP server, which nobody had asked for.|Action: I built a read-only prototype in [two weeks], demoed it to my lead and the release manager, addressed their safety concerns (per-user PATs, approvals kept), and measured before and after.|Result: the team adopted the CIRT MCP server for most release deployments: 6 hours to 2, 6 people to 1.
p9-20.qa: Release deployments needed about 6 people and 6 hours. I proposed automating them through an MCP server, built a read-only prototype in [two weeks], demoed it to my lead and the release manager, addressed their safety concerns (per-user PATs, approvals kept) and measured before and after. The team adopted the CIRT MCP server for most release deployments: 6 hours to 2, 6 people to 1.
i: Influence through a working prototype and data.
Addressed concerns before they became objections.
I measured before and after on [8 vs 8] comparable deployments, which made the case convincing.
f: What was the main objection?
Safety of an AI agent in a regulated release process.
How did you answer it?
Same permissions as the user, confirmations, approvals unchanged, full audit.
wv: I influence decisions with evidence and working software.

p9-21.a: Stay calm and structured: mitigate first, communicate status on a regular cadence, split work clearly when several people help, avoid risky changes under pressure, and do the root-cause work afterwards. Checklists and runbooks reduce panic.
p9-21.qa: I stay calm and structured: mitigate first, communicate status on a regular cadence, split work clearly when several people help, avoid risky changes under pressure, and do the root-cause work afterwards. Checklists and runbooks reduce panic.
i: Example: RabbitMQ outage (recovered all updates the same evening).
Prioritise the most important work, communicate status regularly, and avoid risky shortcuts.
Ask for help early instead of hiding problems.
f: How do you avoid burnout?
Hand over clearly, rotate support and automate repetitive fixes.
What's the worst thing to do under pressure?
Make untested changes in production.

p9-22.a: Lead with impact (who is affected, how badly), then what we are doing and when the next update comes, using plain language and analogies, no jargon; give options with trade-offs when they must decide.
p9-22.qa: Lead with impact (who's affected, how badly), then what we're doing and when the next update comes, in plain language with analogies and no jargon; give options with trade-offs when they must decide.
i: Example: "Some sites see shipment statuses up to 40 minutes old; randomization is unaffected; we expect a fix by 8 pm; next update in 30 minutes."
Use analogies and impact (time, risk, cost), not technical terms.
Offer options with trade-offs and a recommendation.
Example: explaining the RabbitMQ outage as "updates queued and replayed, nothing lost".
f: How do you explain technical debt?
As interest on a loan that slows every future change.
What if you don't know the cause yet?
Say so, share what you're doing and when you'll update.

p9-23.a: An opinionated framework on top of Spring for building Java services quickly: auto-configuration, embedded server (Tomcat), starter dependencies and production features (Actuator). The Java counterpart of ASP.NET Core.
p9-23.qa: Spring Boot is an opinionated framework on top of Spring for building Java services quickly: auto-configuration, an embedded server (Tomcat), starter dependencies and production features (Actuator). It's the Java counterpart of ASP.NET Core.
i: Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17+ and Jakarta EE namespaces; Spring Boot 4 (late 2025) builds on Spring Framework 7.
Actuator ≈ health checks and metrics endpoints.
Spring Boot is an opinionated framework on top of Spring with auto-configuration, embedded servers and starters.
Similar to ASP.NET Core with minimal setup.
f: What is auto-configuration?
Beans configured automatically based on classpath and properties.
Embedded server?
The app runs as a jar with Tomcat inside, like Kestrel.

p9-24.a: The Spring IoC container (ApplicationContext) creates beans and injects their dependencies, like the .NET service provider.|Prefer constructor injection; @Autowired marks an injection point and is optional on a single constructor.
p9-24.qa: The Spring IoC container (ApplicationContext) creates beans and injects their dependencies, like the .NET service provider. Constructor injection is preferred; @Autowired marks an injection point and is optional on a single constructor.
i: Bean scopes: singleton (default), prototype, request, session ≈ .NET singleton, transient, scoped.
@Qualifier ≈ keyed services.
Spring's IoC container creates and wires beans; constructor injection is preferred over field @Autowired.
With one constructor, @Autowired is optional.

Singleton.

Keyed services with [FromKeyedServices].

p9-25.a: All register beans through component scanning. @Component is generic; @Service marks business logic (semantic only); @Repository marks data access and translates database exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException.
p9-25.qa: All three register beans through component scanning. @Component is generic; @Service marks business logic (semantic only); @Repository marks data access and translates database exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy.

@Configuration with @Bean for explicit registrations.

Registering a service with a factory in Program.cs.

p9-26.a: @RestController class with @RequestMapping("/api/shipments"); methods with @GetMapping, @PostMapping; @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody with @Valid; return ResponseEntity with status codes.

p9-28.a: JPA is the Java persistence specification; Hibernate is its most common implementation (the ORM); Spring Data JPA adds repository interfaces that generate queries from method names.|Versus EF Core: similar ideas (entities, change tracking via the persistence context, lazy loading, migrations via Flyway or Liquibase rather than built in); EF Core uses LINQ, JPA uses JPQL or the Criteria API.

Compared with EF Core the ideas are similar (entities, change tracking in the persistence context, lazy loading), but migrations use Flyway or Liquibase, and queries use JPQL or the Criteria API instead of LINQ.
i: N+1 problems exist in both; fetch joins ≈ Include.
@Transactional ≈ explicit transactions or unit of work.
Spring Data JPA generates repositories from interfaces; Hibernate is the JPA implementation.

For security, the Spring Security filter chain, OAuth2 resource server for JWT validation and method security with @PreAuthorize roles.

Spring Security filters ≈ ASP.NET Core middleware.

p9-30.a: Very similar: statically typed, garbage collected, object-oriented.|C# added features earlier (LINQ, async/await, properties, records, pattern matching), has value types and real generics at runtime; Java has a huge ecosystem, virtual threads (Java 21) and runs on many JVM vendors.
p9-30.qa: Java and C# are very similar: statically typed, garbage collected, object-oriented. C# added features earlier (LINQ, async/await, properties, records, pattern matching), has user-defined value types and runtime generics (Java erases generics); Java has a huge ecosystem, virtual threads (Java 21) and many JVM vendors.
i: Java records (16), pattern matching for switch (21).
Virtual threads vs async/await: different models for scalable I/O.
Similar languages; C# has features like LINQ, async/await built in, properties, and value types with structs.
Java has a huge ecosystem and virtual threads (Java 21).

Java generics don't exist at runtime; C# generics do.
Virtual threads?
Lightweight JVM threads letting blocking code scale like async.

p9-31.a: Spring Boot: when the organisation's platform, libraries and people are Java, or a specific JVM ecosystem (big data, certain vendors) matters.|.NET: when the team and code base are .NET, for strong performance, LINQ and EF Core productivity, and first-class Azure and tooling support. p9-31.qa: Choose Spring Boot when the organisation's platform, libraries and people are Java, or a JVM ecosystem (big data, certain vendors) matters; choose .NET when the team and codebase are .NET, for strong performance, LINQ and EF Core productivity, and first-class Azure and tooling support. i: Our [early 2026] upgrade: [3] services, central package management, [10–15%] p95 improvement.

.NET Upgrade Assistant and AI tools help with mechanical changes.
.NET 8: Native AOT for ASP.NET Core, keyed services, TimeProvider; .NET 10: LTS release with C# 14 and further performance gains.

Support lifetimes and stable, planned upgrades in a regulated product.
What broke in your upgrade?
[A few package APIs and analyzer warnings treated as errors], fixed and validated.

Different delivery semantics fit different workloads.

Silent message loss without publisher confirms.

Audit fields, no hard deletes, strict validation and full tests.
